gist: Concludes Atwood's instructions: the working-place must be secret, still and unpolluted by evil associates or lingering imaginative impressions; Vaughan's 'lessons' prescribe self-examination, moderate heat, charity, piety, solitude and perseverance; Atwood then ends her 'suggestive' introduction, saying the end is implied in the beginning and the rest must come from practice and the Master Key.

notes.point: Secrecy was a principal aim, hard to combine with other conditions varying with the spiritual guide; a locality like Virgil's for his Bees, without evil associates, is desirable.
Air currents disturb communion; imaginative impressures absorbed by the entranced Subject linger and pollute a place's ether (adepts, Cornelius Agrippa). A fitting working-place is a grace.

Vaughan's lessons, adopted as conclusion: examine yourself; you co-operate with God. Excess heat divides the Chaos; the Quintessence leaves violent hands. Speak little. Knowing the First Matter finds Nature's Sanctuary; only the Door remains.

Vaughan: charity nurses faith; heart in heaven, hands on earth; live heavenly to commune with superiors; be one, not alone; day as contracted year; indeterminate agents until a determinate one; avoid extremes; perseverance ends in miracles.
Enough for suggestive purposes. Perseverance ranks next to benevolence and right intention; effects lead to causes; as in a seed, the end is implied in the beginning.
The introduction to the Sphinx’s lair ends; applying the Master Key moves the first vital cause; practice opens the rest.

method.veiled: Secrecy having been a principal object with those practicing this Art
method.plain: Practitioners aimed above all at keeping the work secret, which was often hard to secure together with the other required conditions.
method.basis: III.4 ¶42 states it directly.

method.veiled: the other conditions, which vary with the constitution and instinct of the spiritual guide
method.plain: The proper conditions of the work are not fixed but depend on the constitution and instinct of the 'spiritual guide'; the chunk does not say who or what the guide is.
method.basis: III.4 ¶42 only; see ambiguities for the identity of the 'spiritual guide'.

method.veiled: It is a grace - To finde a fitting working-place.
method.plain: The work needs a suitable place, like the locality Virgil appointed for his Bees, kept free of corrupt and evil associates (exclusions the text calls 'allegorical') and of strong air currents.
method.basis: III.4 ¶42 calls such a locality 'desirable' and names the exclusions as allegorical; ¶43 gives the verse. The chunk does not describe Virgil's locality further or decode the allegory.

also.text: Just such a locality as Virgil appointed for his Bees, has been mentioned as desirable with all his appropriate allegorical exceptions of corrupt and evil associates

method.veiled: Strong currents of air are well known to disturb communion
method.plain: Draughts or wind in the working-place disturb the 'communion' the work depends on; this chunk does not define communion.
method.basis: III.4 ¶42 states it directly.

method.veiled: the entranced Subject is more or less susceptible of all imaginative impressures, which, even after their act has passed away, hang and pollute the ether of their pertinacious abode
method.plain: The person in trance (the 'Subject') takes in imaginative impressions; these linger in a place after the act that produced them and contaminate its 'ether', so the place must be clean of such residues.
method.basis: III.4 ¶42 states susceptibility and lingering pollution, citing adepts and Cornelius Agrippa.

method.veiled: consider well with thyself what manner of man thou art, and what it is that thou wouldst do: For it is no small matter.
method.plain: Before attempting the practice, the operator must examine his own character, intention, knowledge and practice.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 direct precepts.
method.voice: QUOTED: Vaughan (endorsed by Atwood as 'lessons of an English Adept')

also.text: let him first examine his knowledge, and especially his practice

method.veiled: Thou hast resolved with thyself to be a co-operator with the living God, and to minister to Him in his work of generation.
method.plain: The operator does not make the result himself; he assists God's own generative work and must not hinder it.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44, followed by 'Have a care, therefore, that thou dost not hinder his work'.

also.text: Have a care, therefore, that thou dost not hinder his work

method.veiled: if thy heat exceeds the natural proportion, thou hast stirred up the wrath of the moist natures, and they will stand up against the central fire
method.plain: Applying 'heat' beyond the natural proportion sets the moist natures and the central fire against each other and divides the Chaos; the passage ties this failure to the operator's violent handling. What the heat literally is, is not said.
method.basis: Consequences stated in III.4 ¶44; the link to operator violence rests on 'thy violent destructive Hands', 'a few violent knocks' and 'charitable and not destructive to thyself' in the same paragraph. See ambiguities.

also.text: there will be a terrible division in the Chaos

method.veiled: the sweet spirit of Peace, the true eternal Quintessence, will depart from the elements, leaving both of them and thee to confusion
method.plain: The Quintessence, identified with the 'spirit of Peace', abides in the elements; under violent handling it withdraws and will not act on the Matter, leaving matter and operator in confusion.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44: the apposition asserts the identity; departure and refusal to 'apply himself' are stated.

also.text: neither will he apply himself to that Matter as long as it is in thy violent destructive Hands

method.veiled: Nature gave us one tongue and two ears, that we might hear much and speak little
method.plain: The operator should listen and learn much and speak little, not publishing his ignorance.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 draws this application explicitly.

also.text: Let not any man therefore be ready to vomit forth his own shame and ignorance

method.veiled: lest upon the experience of a few violent knocks he presume to judge of Nature in her very sobrieties
method.plain: Failures from forcing the work are no basis for judging how Nature works when handled gently.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 contrasts 'violent knocks' with Nature's 'sobrieties', following the warning against excess heat and violent hands.

method.veiled: if thou knowest the principal First Matter, know also for certain thou hast discovered the Sanctuary of Nature
method.plain: Knowing the First Matter is equivalent to having found the inner seat of Nature's treasures.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 asserts the equivalence directly.

method.veiled: There is nothing between thee and her treasures but the Door: that indeed must be opened.
method.plain: Once the First Matter is known, one further step remains: opening a 'Door' to Nature's treasures. This chunk does not explain the Door.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 sequence: First Matter known = Sanctuary found; only the Door remains.

method.veiled: Have therefore a charitable seraphic mind, charitable and not destructive to thyself.
method.plain: The operator needs a charitable disposition: charitable works produce hope of heaven, hope produces faith; works of darkness yield no hope and only the devils' faith 'to believe and tremble'.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 gives the chain charity -> hope -> faith explicitly.

also.text: as God is the Father, so Charity is the nurse of Faith

method.veiled: Have thy heart in heaven and thy hands upon earth. Ascend in piety and descend in charity.
method.plain: The operator keeps his mind directed upward while his practical work stays on earth, rising by piety and turning outward in charity; this is called 'the Nature of Light'.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44: 'For this is the Nature of Light and the way of the children of it.'

also.text: Settle not in the lees and puddles of the world.

method.veiled: You must live, as says Agrippa, according to God and the angels, rejecting all things that are dissimilar to the heaven; otherwise thou canst have no communion with superiors.
method.plain: Communion with higher powers requires a way of life made like heaven, rejecting what is unlike it.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 states the condition.

method.veiled: Unus esto non solus. Avoid the multitude, as well of passions as of persons.
method.plain: The operator should be inwardly unified, not merely alone, withdrawing from crowds both of people and of passions.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44: the following English sentence is read as glossing the Latin (not marked as a gloss); 'inwardly unified' rests partly on our translation.

method.veiled: every day is a contracted year, and that each year is an extended day. Anticipate the year in the day, and lose not a day in the year.
method.plain: A day and a year are treated as the same cycle, contracted and extended; how this applies to the work is not explained in this chunk.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 only; see ambiguities.

method.veiled: Make use of indeterminate agents till thou canst find a determinate one: the many wish well, but one only loves.
method.plain: Work with general, non-specific agents until the one specific agent is found; the chunk identifies neither.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 only; contrast 'the many' / 'one only'. See ambiguities.

method.veiled: Circumferences spread, but centers contract; so superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate
method.plain: Higher things dissolve (expand, as a circumference spreads), lower things coagulate (condense, as a center contracts).
method.basis: III.4 ¶44: the 'so' states the analogy directly.

method.veiled: stand not long in the sun nor long in the shade, where extremes meet, there look for complexions
method.plain: Avoid staying in either extreme; the 'complexions' sought appear where extremes meet. This chunk does not say what the complexions are.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 only; fits the earlier warning against heat exceeding 'the natural proportion'.

method.veiled: There is nothing stronger than Perseverance, for it ends in miracles
method.plain: Persistence, learning from errors and misfortunes, is essential; after benevolence and right intention it is the requirement most insisted on.
method.basis: III.4 ¶44 (Vaughan) and III.4 ¶45 (Atwood) state it.

also.text: Nothing is more generally insisted on, next to benevolence and rectitude of intention, than perseverance for this experiment
Learn from thy errors to be infallible, and from they misfortunes to be constant.

method.veiled: effects rationally investigated lead into their causes
method.plain: Reasoned study of effects leads back to their causes.
method.basis: III.4 ¶45 direct statement.

method.veiled: in this philosophy the end is implied in the beginning, and the purpose is by the product made manifest
method.plain: As a seed grows according to its species in congenial soil, the outcome of the work is contained in its start; the product reveals the purpose, proceeding from motive through action and a metaphysical cause into a physical effect.
method.basis: III.4 ¶45 gives the seed analogy and the chain motive -> action -> metaphysical cause -> physical effect.

also.text: the motive, through the resulting action, by the metaphysical cause, into physical effect

method.veiled: The first link in the chain of vital causes moves, as we apply the Master Key.
method.plain: Applying the 'Master Key' sets the chain of vital causes in motion; this chunk does not say what the Master Key is.
method.basis: III.4 ¶47 only.

method.veiled: Portus Explicit, at Praxis manaulis caetera pandet.
method.plain: The introductory part ends; the remainder is to be learned by hands-on practice.
method.basis: III.4 ¶48 (our translation) with ¶45 'without practical information' and ¶47 'we conclude our introduction'.

sources.use: Supports the need for a fitting working-place.

ambiguities.quote: the constitution and instinct of the spiritual guide
readings: A human director of the work, paired with the entranced Subject, whose own constitution sets the conditions.
A guiding spirit or spiritual influence active in the work.
ambiguities.basis: III.4 ¶42 gives no further description; the same paragraph's 'entranced Subject' suggests a guide/subject pair, while 'communion' and 'spiritual' fit either.

ambiguities.quote: if thy heat exceeds the natural proportion
readings: Literal heat applied in an operation.
The operator's own vehemence or violence of handling.
ambiguities.basis: Fire/moist natures language supports the first; 'thy violent destructive Hands', 'a few violent knocks' and 'charitable and not destructive to thyself' (III.4 ¶44) support the second. The text does not gloss 'heat'.

ambiguities.quote: every day is a contracted year, and that each year is an extended day
readings: A rule of diligence: use each day fully ('lose not a day in the year').
A correspondence in the work's process: a short cycle reproduces the long one in small ('Anticipate the year in the day').
ambiguities.basis: Both rest on the following sentence in III.4 ¶44; 'contracted'/'extended' also parallels 'centers contract'/'Circumferences spread' in the same paragraph, favouring the second.

ambiguities.quote: Make use of indeterminate agents till thou canst find a determinate one: the many wish well, but one only loves.
readings: Agents in the operation: general means until the one specific agent is found.
Persons: many well-wishers versus one who truly loves, i.e. a single devoted helper or guide.
ambiguities.basis: 'agents' suggests the operation; 'the many wish well, but one only loves' and the preceding 'Avoid the multitude, as well of passions as of persons' suggest persons.

ambiguities.quote: the practice (that is of the ultimate Philosophic Work)
readings: Atwood's interpolated gloss within the quotation.
ambiguities.basis: The parenthesis precedes 'says Vaughan'; the text does not mark whose words it is.

ambiguities.quote: Portus Explicit, at Praxis manaulis caetera pandet.
readings: 'Explicit' as the conventional closing word: 'Here ends the harbour/approach'.
ambiguities.basis: III.4 ¶47 says the introduction is concluded; ¶45 says more words are of little use 'without practical information'. Both readings rest on our translation.

translations.translation: He who grasps it, he is wise.

translations.original: Portus Explicit, at Praxis manaulis caetera pandet.
translations.translation: Here ends the approach (harbour); but manual practice will lay open the rest.

threads.note: 'has been mentioned as desirable' points back to an earlier mention of a locality like Virgil's for his Bees.
'the foregoing instructions' refers back to the instructions given before this point (not specified here).
Atwood calls everything so far an 'introduction ... to the Sphinx’s lair' and says the first vital cause moves 'as we apply the Master Key', pointing forward to the practice.
Latin close (our translation): manual practice will lay open 'the rest'.
